newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity has no plans to close Magellan Fund.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity has no plans to close Magellan Fund.

text.p: Fidelity Investments has no plans to close its massive Magellan Fund or cut its three percent load, Fidelity executives told fund holders at a meeting in Boston late on Thursday.
"No," said Gary Burkhead, president of Fidelity Management and Research Co, when asked by a member of the audience of about 2,000 if Fidelity would close the fund.
Paul Hondros, president of Fidelity's retail group, when asked by reporters after the event if the load would be cut, replied, "No."
Burkhead told the audience on the last leg of Fidelity's six city tour over the last two weeks that Magellan's $54 billion in assets has not hurt the fund's performance.
He said the "size of the fund in no way affects performance," and said that the key is to buy the right stocks.
Magellan Fund manager Bob Stansky, who took over the fund last June, said it did take time to adjust to running such a large fund compared to his previous fund, Fidelity Growth Company Fund.
"Fifteen billion dollars is not $55 billion, I'll be the first to admit. It took a little time to get used to it, yes," he said.

Stansky has cut back on Magellan's heavy exposure to bonds and cash when he took over to 7.9 percent of total assets in bonds and 3.6 percent in cash as of November 30, the most recent date figures are available.
He told the audience the portfolio was "fully invested in equites" but did not elaborate.

In an interview in a Fidelity brochure distributed to the audience, he said, "I've looked at the combination of cash and bonds in this low-interest rate environment and I think it's safe to say that my target is to be about five percent total non-equities."
Stansky also told the audience that he thinks bank stocks could benefit from mergers and acquisitions in the near term.
"I think we'll see a lot of acquisitions going forward," he said. The quickest way for banks to improve their revenues is to merge with another bank and then cut overhead costs, he said.
Magellan had 8.7 percent of its assets at the end of November invested in finance stocks, up from 5.8 percent at the end of May.

Despite the poor return at Magellan, due in part to its large bond holdings of 19.3 percent of assets when Stansky took it over, he said he is not pressured by management to buy certain stocks or sectors.
Stansky said that Magellan is being run in the same way that previous managers such as Peter Lynch and Morris Smith ran the fund, by buying companies whose earnings are consistently growing.
Burkhead said Stansky has done "a really good job in repositioning" Magellan.
"I think that fund is well positioned for 1997," he added.
